units.t: Maths Shorts.

In this episode: Nature's geometry: hexagons, spirals and bubbles, Logarithms: the invention that turned multiplying into adding, Ramanujan: the clerk who wrote to Cambridge and Calculus without fear: the maths of change.
Part one. Nature's geometry: hexagons, spirals and bubbles.
Bees build hexagons, sunflowers count in Fibonacci numbers and soap bubbles solve maths problems in an instant.
Nature is full of geometry, and there are good reasons why.
The bee's hexagon.
Honeycomb is made of near-perfect hexagons.
Only three regular shapes fit together on a flat surface with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons.
Of these, hexagons enclose a given area with the shortest total wall.
For cells of equal area, a square needs about 7.
5 per cent more perimeter than a hexagon, and a triangle about 22 per cent more.
Bees must eat honey to make wax, so saving wax saves energy.
Around 300 CE Pappus of Alexandria praised bees for their geometric wisdom.
The stronger claim, that hexagons beat every possible way of dividing a flat surface into equal areas, was only proved in 1999, by the mathematician Thomas Hales.
It is known as the honeycomb conjecture.
Sunflower spirals.
Look closely at a large sunflower and you will see seeds in two sets of spirals, one clockwise and one anticlockwise.
Count them and you often get neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55, or 55 and 89.
Pinecones, pineapples and daisy centres show smaller pairs, like 8 and 13.
The pattern is common rather than universal.
A large citizen science project published in 2016, inspired by Alan Turing's interest in sunflowers, counted the spirals on hundreds of seed heads.
A sizeable minority did not fit simple Fibonacci patterns.
Nature leans strongly towards these numbers, but it is not an unbreakable rule.
The golden angle.
A sunflower head grows from the centre, adding seeds one at a time, each at a fixed angle from the one before.
If that angle were a simple fraction of a turn, such as a quarter, seeds would line up in four straight spokes with big gaps between them.
The angle that best avoids lining up is about 137.
5 degrees, called the golden angle.
It is linked to the golden ratio, the number that resists approximation by simple fractions more than any other.
With it, seeds fill the head evenly and pack in as many as possible.
The spirals we see, and their Fibonacci counts, are a side effect of that efficient packing, and computer models reproduce them from this one rule.
Bubbles solve problems.
Blow a single soap bubble and it becomes a sphere.
For any amount of air, a sphere has the smallest possible surface, and surface tension pulls the soap film as tight as it can go.
When bubbles cluster in a foam, they follow rules set out by the Belgian physicist Joseph Plateau in 1873.
Soap films always meet in threes, at equal angles of 120 degrees, and the edges where films meet always come together in fours, at about 109.
5 degrees.
Dip a wire frame into soapy water and the film often forms the smallest surface spanning it, instantly solving a problem that can take pages of calculation.
The architect Frei Otto used soap film models to design light, curving roofs.
Spirals, size and stone.
A snail or nautilus cannot remodel its shell, so it adds material at the open end and each turn is a scaled-up copy of the last.
The result is close to a logarithmic spiral, which keeps its shape however far you zoom.
Jacob Bernoulli called it the 'marvellous spiral' and asked for it on his gravestone, though the mason carved the wrong kind.
Claims that the nautilus follows the golden ratio do not survive careful measurement.
Geometry also limits size.
Double an ant's length, width and height and its leg strength rises four times, but its weight rises eight.
Galileo described this square-cube law in 1638, which is why elephants have stout legs.
Slowly cooling lava cracks at angles near 120 degrees into columns, as at the Giant's Causeway and Organ Pipes National Park near Melbourne.
The key idea: Hexagons enclose a given area with the least wall, so bees save wax by building them.
Part two. Logarithms: the invention that turned multiplying into adding.
In 1614 a Scottish nobleman published tables that saved astronomers years of drudgery.
For the next 350 years, his idea sat in the pocket of every engineer as the slide rule.
The drudgery of multiplying.
Picture an astronomer around 1600 working out a planet's orbit.
Each step means multiplying and dividing numbers of seven or more digits, and one slip ruins weeks of work.
Navigators and surveyors faced the same burden.
Adding large numbers is quick and fairly safe, but multiplying by hand means rows of partial products and lots of carrying.
Mathematicians wondered whether hard multiplication could become easy addition.
A clue came from powers.
Since 2 times 2 times 2 is 8 and 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 is 16, multiplying 8 by 16 means adding the counts of twos, 3 plus 4, to get 7 twos.
That is 128.
Napier's idea.
John Napier was the Laird of Merchiston near Edinburgh, who also wrote a fiercely argued book on the Book of Revelation.
Mathematics was his passion.
He spent around two decades developing logarithms, a word built from Greek roots meaning ratio and number, and published them in 1614.
His tables paired numbers with their logarithms.
Napier's version differs from today's, but the essential trick was there.
With base 10, the logarithm of 100 is 2 and of 1,000 is 3.
The logarithm of 2 is about 0.
301 and of 8 about 0.
Add them to get 1.
204, look up the number with that logarithm, and you find 16, which is 2 times 8.
Division becomes subtraction, powers become multiplication, and square roots become halving.
Briggs and Kepler.
The English mathematician Henry Briggs travelled to Scotland in 1615 to meet Napier.
They agreed that logarithms would be more convenient in base 10, so the logarithm of 10 was 1 and of 100 was 2.
Napier died in 1617.
Briggs calculated the new tables by hand, including a large volume in 1624.
These common logarithms stayed in classrooms, including Australian ones, until cheap electronic calculators arrived in the 1970s.
The astronomer Johannes Kepler seized on logarithms early.
He used them in completing the Rudolphine Tables, published in 1627, which predicted planetary positions far more accurately than anything before.
Logarithms did not create the scientific revolution, but they made its endless calculations bearable.
The slide rule.
Soon after Napier, the English mathematician Edmund Gunter drew a ruler marked with a logarithmic scale, so distances along it represented logarithms.
Using dividers, users could add lengths and so multiply numbers.
In the 1620s and 1630s the clergyman William Oughtred slid two such scales against each other, which did the adding automatically.
This was the slide rule.
For centuries it was the engineer's constant companion, helping design bridges, ships, aircraft and, at NASA, the rockets of the Apollo programme.
A good slide rule gave about three significant figures, accurate enough for most engineering.
Pocket calculators replaced it almost overnight in the 1970s.
Logarithms today.
Calculators made log tables obsolete, but logarithms are everywhere.
The decibel scale for sound is logarithmic: every 10 decibels means ten times the sound intensity.
Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic, as is the pH scale, where each step is a tenfold change.
In finance and biology, logarithms describe compound growth and halving.
Your senses seem to work roughly logarithmically too, noticing proportional changes rather than absolute ones.
An extra candle brightens a dark room far more than a sunny one.
The idea Napier spent twenty years refining still shapes how scientists see the world, long after its original purpose disappeared.
The key idea: Adding is easy and multiplying is hard, and patterns in powers hint at a way to turn one into the other.
Part three. Ramanujan: the clerk who wrote to Cambridge.
A largely self-taught clerk in Madras posted pages of strange formulas to a famous English mathematician.
They were so astonishing that they changed both men's lives.
A borrowed book.
Srinivasa Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 in Erode, in southern India, and grew up in Kumbakonam.
As a teenager he found a book by George Shoobridge Carr, a summary of several thousand mathematical results, mostly given without proofs.
He worked through it alone, filling notebooks with his own discoveries.
His obsession had a cost.
He won a college scholarship but neglected his other subjects, failed his exams and lost it.
For several years he lived in poverty, working with little guidance.
Eventually supporters who recognised his talent helped him find a job as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust in 1912, giving him a small wage and time to keep working.
The letter to Cambridge.
In January 1913 Ramanujan wrote to Godfrey Harold Hardy, a leading mathematician at Trinity College, Cambridge, enclosing pages of formulas, many about infinite series, without proof.
Hardy got many letters from cranks and was tempted to dismiss it.
But he and John Littlewood realised the pages were remarkable: some results known, a few wrong, many new and astonishing.
Hardy said some must be true, because no one would have had the imagination to invent them otherwise.
Ramanujan sailed for England in 1914.
Hardy insisted on rigorous proofs, while Ramanujan reached results by intuition, saying some came from his family goddess Namagiri.
Wartime Cambridge was hard for a strict vegetarian far from home, yet in 1918 he became a Fellow of the Royal Society, one of the first Indians so honoured.
The taxicab number.
The most famous story comes from Hardy.
Visiting his friend in hospital, Hardy remarked that he had arrived in taxi number 1729, which seemed a rather dull number.
Ramanujan replied that, on the contrary, it was very interesting.
It is the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.
Check it: 1 cubed plus 12 cubed is 1 plus 1,728, which is 1,729.
And 9 cubed plus 10 cubed is 729 plus 1,000, which is also 1,729.
Numbers with this property are now called taxicab numbers.
The story captures something real about Ramanujan, who knew individual numbers like old friends.
Breaking numbers into pieces.
One of their greatest achievements concerns partitions, the ways to write a whole number as a sum of positive whole numbers.
The number 4 has five: 4, 3 plus 1, 2 plus 2, 2 plus 1+1 and 1 plus 1+1 plus 1.
Counts explode as numbers grow.
The number 200 has 3,972,999,029,388, a figure Percy MacMahon worked out painstakingly by hand.
Hardy and Ramanujan found a formula that estimated such values with astonishing accuracy, later refined into an exact formula.
Ramanujan also spotted hidden patterns.
The partition counts of 4, 9, 14, 19, 24 and so on, every fifth number, are always divisible by 5.
Those counts begin 5, 30, 135, 490 and 1,575.
A short life, long legacy.
By 1917 Ramanujan was seriously ill.
The cause is still debated; tuberculosis and a liver infection, amoebiasis, have both been suggested.
He returned to India in 1919, still working on ‘mock theta functions’, and died on 26 April 1920, aged 32.
In 1976 George Andrews found a bundle of later papers, the ‘lost notebook’, in Trinity's library.
Researchers spent decades proving its results, and some ideas have found uses in modern physics.
His 1914 formulas for pi later helped computers calculate millions of digits.
India celebrates 22 December as National Mathematics Day.
His story is also a warning: he was found partly by luck, through supporters and one letter that reached the right reader.
Hardy wondered how much more he might have achieved with an earlier, fuller education.
The key idea: Ramanujan taught himself mathematics from a book of results with few proofs, at the cost of his formal education.
Part four. Calculus without fear: the maths of change.
Calculus has a fearsome reputation, but its two big ideas can be grasped with a speedometer and an odometer.
Its invention also sparked one of the bitterest feuds in science.
Two simple questions.
Strip away the symbols and calculus asks two questions.
How fast is something changing at this exact moment?
And if you know how fast it is changing, how much has it added up to over time?
Every car shows both ideas.
The speedometer reports how fast your distance is changing right now.
The odometer adds up all those changing speeds into a total distance.
The first idea is differentiation, which gives a derivative.
The second is integration, which gives an integral.
Together they sit at the heart of physics, engineering, economics and biology, anywhere things change smoothly.
Ordinary arithmetic copes with fixed values.
Calculus copes with constant change.
Ancient near-misses.
Long before anyone named calculus, the Greeks wrestled with its core difficulty.
Around the fifth century BCE, Zeno of Elea argued that swift Achilles can never catch a tortoise with a head start, since each time he reaches where it was, it has moved on.
How can infinitely many steps add up to a finite result?
Today we can answer: a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on forever totals exactly 1.
In the third century BCE, Archimedes squeezed a circle between polygons inside and outside it.
With 96 sides, he showed pi lies between 223/71 and 22/7, about 3.
He used similar reasoning for the area under a parabola and the volume of a sphere.
He lacked a general method.
Newton versus Leibniz.
In the mid-1660s, with Cambridge closed by plague, young Isaac Newton developed his method of fluxions but kept it largely to himself.
In Germany, Gottfried Leibniz developed his own version in the 1670s and published first, in 1684.
A bitter priority dispute followed, with Newton's supporters accusing Leibniz of plagiarism.
In 1712 the Royal Society, which Newton led as president, ruled in Newton's favour in a report he secretly drafted much of himself.
Historians now agree the two men invented calculus independently.
Leibniz's notation, such as dy/dx and the long S for an integral, proved clearer and won out.
British mathematicians, loyal to Newton's dots, fell behind continental Europe for decades.
Zooming and slicing.
Drop a ball and it falls about 4.
9 times t² metres in t seconds, ignoring air resistance.
How fast is it moving at exactly one second?
From 1 to 1.
1 seconds, the average speed is 10.
29 metres per second.
From 1 to 1.
01, it is about 9.
As the interval shrinks, the average closes in on exactly 9.
That limit is the derivative: the slope of a curve at a single point.
Integration runs the other way.
A steady 60 kilometres an hour for two hours is a rectangle on a speed graph, 60 high and 2 wide, so 120 kilometres.
For varying speed, slice the area into thin strips and add them up.
Infinitely thin strips give the exact answer.
Engineers use this for forces on dams and volumes of fuel tanks.
Why calculus took over.
The deepest discovery is that the two halves undo each other.
Integrate a speed to get distance, differentiate that, and you get the speed back.
This is the fundamental theorem of calculus.
Isaac Barrow, Newton's teacher, had glimpsed it, but Newton and Leibniz made it a working method.
Instead of adding thousands of strips, you find a formula whose derivative matches your curve, and the area follows almost instantly.
Yet the foundations were shaky.
In 1734 George Berkeley mocked vanishing quantities as ‘ghosts of departed quantities’.
In the nineteenth century, Cauchy and Weierstrass rebuilt calculus on precisely defined limits, answering Zeno at last.
Today it underpins weather forecasts, rocket trajectories, medical scanners and AI training, which follows derivatives downhill to reduce errors.
The key idea: Calculus answers two questions: how fast something is changing right now, and how much has built up over time.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do bees build hexagonal cells?
Answer. They need the least wall, which saves wax.
Question two. Using powers of 2, why does 8 times 16 equal 128?
Answer. Three twos and four twos make seven twos.
Question three. What did Ramanujan's obsession with mathematics cost him?
Answer. His formal education.
Question four. In the car picture of calculus, what does the odometer represent?
Answer. Adding up changing speeds into a total distance.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
